lessons.title: Building an aquaculture budget
lessons.html:
What a budget does

A budget is a financial plan for a period, usually a year or a production cycle. It forecasts income and costs so the farm can see whether it will make a profit, when cash will be short and what it can afford to invest. On a fish farm, where money goes out for months before any fish are sold, cash flow planning is as important as profit.

Income

Estimate harvest volume per unit from stocking numbers, expected survival and expected harvest weight. Multiply by the expected price per kilogram for each market channel (live sales, fresh whole fish, processors). Be conservative; use recent actual survival and prices, not best-case figures.

Variable costs

  • Feed: usually the largest cost. Estimate from expected weight gain x feed conversion ratio x price per tonne.
  • Fingerlings or fry.
  • Electricity and fuel for pumps, aerators and generators.
  • Oxygen, lime, salt, disinfectants and remedies.
  • Harvest, ice, packaging and transport.
  • Casual labour for peak periods.

Fixed costs

  • Permanent salaries and wages.
  • Insurance, licences and permits, water use charges.
  • Maintenance and repairs.
  • Depreciation on tanks, pumps, generators and vehicles.
  • Interest on loans.

Worked example

ItemCalculationAmount
Fish produced20 000 kg
Feed20 000 kg x FCR 1.6 x R14/kgR448 000
Income20 000 kg x R45/kgR900 000

These figures are for illustration only; use your farm's actual prices. The example shows how strongly FCR drives profit: at FCR 2.0 the feed bill rises to R560 000.

Cash flow budget

Spread income and costs month by month. Feed costs climb as fish grow, while income arrives only at harvest. The cash flow shows when you need an overdraft or must stagger stocking to spread harvests.

lessons.title: Procurement principles
lessons.html:
Buying the right inputs at the right price

Procurement is the process of obtaining goods and services: feed, fingerlings, equipment, spares, chemicals and contractors. Good procurement balances price, quality, reliability and risk.

The procurement cycle

  1. Identify the need from the production plan and stock levels.
  2. Specify exactly what is needed: feed type, protein content, pellet size, quantity, delivery date.
  3. Source and compare: obtain written quotations from more than one supplier for significant purchases.
  4. Approve according to the farm's authority limits.
  5. Order with a written purchase order.
  6. Receive and inspect: check quantity, condition, batch numbers and expiry dates against the order and delivery note.
  7. Pay only against a matched order, delivery note and invoice.
  8. Review supplier performance.

Choosing suppliers

  • Feed: consistency matters more than a small price saving; poor feed raises FCR and can cause disease. Check registration of feeds under Act 36 of 1947 where applicable.
  • Fingerlings: buy from reputable hatcheries with good health history and the right permits; cheap, unhealthy seed stock is the most expensive mistake a farm can make.
  • Equipment: consider spares availability, service support and energy use, not only purchase price.

Controls against loss and fraud

  • Separate duties: the person who orders should not be the only person who receives and approves payment.
  • Keep stock cards and do regular stock counts.
  • Declare conflicts of interest with suppliers.

Budget control

Compare actual spending with the budget every month. Investigate variances: is feed spend higher because fish grew faster (good) or because FCR worsened (bad)? Adjust plans early.

Key points

  • Feed is usually the largest cost and depends heavily on FCR.
  • Prepare a monthly cash flow, not only an annual profit budget.
  • Specify needs clearly and get competing written quotes.
  • Match order, delivery note and invoice before paying.
  • Compare actual to budget monthly and explain variances.
